output.title: Before-and-after framing skips the hard part
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to accept the outcome before the middle has been checked. But the middle is where the real decision lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the gap between a demo and daily use. That gap is often where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For an owner who has tried ChatGPT but not wired AI into a real process, the useful question is not “Will AI do it?” It is: is this workflow repeated often enough to test? Bareni’s free 30-minute diagnostic is built for that boundary. It identifies one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to keep the decision tied to a real process.

A practical next step is simple: pick one weekly workflow and write down what success would have to show before you commit. If you cannot state that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
